analysis.one_liner: Bans partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts and lets voters sue to stop it.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or action, and it closed the session with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit states from drawing congressional district maps that unduly favor or disfavor a political party, banning the use of party registration, voting history, precinct election results, and incumbent addresses when drawing new districts after each census. Any eligible voter in a state could sue to have a partisan map thrown out, with courts able to appoint a special master to redraw the map. Maps drawn by bipartisan redistricting commissions would get a presumption of validity, encouraging states to take map-drawing away from partisan legislatures.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters in states where congressional maps are drawn by whichever party controls the state legislature, so that a party can win most of the seats with a minority of the votes. Voters whose districts are shaped to protect a particular incumbent would also gain, since districts would have to be drawn without regard to where incumbents live.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans states from drawing congressional districts that unduly favor or disfavor a political party, and prohibits using party registration, voter history, precinct election results, or incumbent addresses as criteria.
Any eligible voter could sue to invalidate a partisan districting plan before a three-judge federal court, and courts could appoint a special master to redraw the map.
Maps created by nonpartisan or bipartisan redistricting commissions would receive a rebuttable presumption of validity, giving states an incentive to move map-drawing out of partisan legislatures.

analysis.who_pays: The political parties and incumbent officeholders who currently gain from map-drawing power would lose the ability to lock in favorable districts. States would also face litigation risk from voter lawsuits, and taxpayers could bear the cost of court-appointed special masters redrawing maps.

drawbacks.text: Determining whether a map 'unduly favors' a party depends on statistical measures of partisan bias, a contested area of social science; the bill lets courts consider 'statistical evidence of the extent and durability of partisan bias,' which could invite endless litigation over where to draw the line.
The bill applies only to congressional districts, not state legislative districts, so it would leave half of the gerrymandering problem untouched.

In most cases courts would fix a bad map by appointing a special master rather than creating citizen-drawn districts, so the remedy runs through courts and lawyers rather than through the people themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: maps drawn by the party in power can let politicians pick their voters, and the courts' own rules against partisan gerrymandering were unsettled at the time. The main cost is litigation and reliance on court-appointed experts to fix bad maps, and the remedy is indirect. The bill would not have made any sitting Congress less dependent on the maps it was elected under, since it applies to future redistricting cycles.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it once, referred it to the Judiciary Committee, and nobody ever moved it to a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the Fair Maps Act of 2018 on June 25, 2018, with no cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

The bill would have prohibited states from drawing congressional district plans that unduly favor or disfavor a political party, established required, prohibited, and permissible districting criteria, and allowed any eligible voter to sue to invalidate a partisan plan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The political parties and incumbents who benefit from partisan maps kept their advantage, since no state's districting practices changed. Nothing was put to a vote, so the status quo in map-drawing survived intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Parties and incumbents who draw the maps

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate; it had no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to and never reported from
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action; the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, and no Senate floor action of any kind occurred after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator supported the bill and none opposed it on the record; with zero cosponsors, the Senate never took up the question, and no roll call exists to show how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislative majorities that draw maps
industries.note: The bill died, so map-drawing politicians kept the ability to shape their own districts around party registration, voter history, and their own addresses. Gerrymandering is not an industry in the usual sense, but it is a concentrated political interest the bill would have taken power from.

industries.industry: Election-law litigators and political redistricting consultants
industries.note: Had the bill passed, its voter-suit provision and statistical tests would have generated substantial litigation and map-drawing consulting work. The bill's death preserved that marketplace in its existing form rather than creating it.
